title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Control in Patients with Previous Ischemic Stroke
abstract: BACKGROUND: The optimal systolic blood-pressure (SBP) target for secondary prevention after ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA) is uncertain, and previous trials have not established whether a target below 120 mm Hg is superior to the conventional target below 140 mm Hg in this population. OPTIMAL-STROKE (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04036409) was designed to address this question. METHODS: OPTIMAL-STROKE was an investigator-initiated, multicenter, randomized, open-label trial with blinded endpoint adjudication by a clinical events committee, conducted at 30 sites in Brazil, with enrollment from August 2019 through August 2022. Eligible patients had a previous ischemic stroke or TIA, were clinically stable for at least 48 hours, and had elevated SBP (reported as a range of 130 to 180 mm Hg). Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to intensive treatment targeting an SBP of less than 120 mm Hg or to standard treatment targeting an SBP of less than 140 mm Hg, using open-label antihypertensive therapy. The primary outcome was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure. A total of 4,368 patients were randomly assigned: 2,172 to intensive treatment and 2,196 to standard treatment. RESULTS: Mean SBP after the first 3 months was 122.0 mm Hg in the intensive-treatment group and 135.2 mm Hg in the standard-treatment group, a between-group separation of approximately 13 mm Hg. Over a median follow-up of 3.9 years, the primary composite outcome occurred in 236 patients (10.9%) in the intensive-treatment group and in 297 patients (13.5%) in the standard-treatment group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.67 to 0.94; P=0.007). This corresponds to an absolute between-group difference of 2.6 percentage points and a relative risk reduction of approximately 21%. With respect to safety, rates of serious adverse events, orthostatic hypotension and injuries were similar in the two groups, whereas renal events were more frequent with intensive treatment, a finding the investigators attributed mainly to a hemodynamic reduction in estimated glomerular filtration rate. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with previous ischemic stroke or TIA and elevated blood pressure, targeting an SBP of less than 120 mm Hg reduced the incidence of major cardiovascular events as compared with a target of less than 140 mm Hg. The investigators call for individualized treatment and careful monitoring of renal function, given the excess of renal events in the intensive-treatment group. The American Heart Association describes the findings as preliminary until peer-reviewed publication is fully disseminated.

title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Lowering in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes
abstract: BACKGROUND: Whether a systolic blood-pressure (SBP) target below 120 mm Hg reduces cardiovascular events in patients with type 2 diabetes remains contested: ACCORD-BP was neutral whereas the more recent BPROAD trial in China was positive. OPTIMAL-DIABETES (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04040634) was designed to test an intensive target in an ethnically diverse, high-cardiovascular-risk diabetic population. METHODS: OPTIMAL-DIABETES was a multicenter, randomized, open-label trial conducted in Brazil. Eligible patients were adults (reported as 50 years of age or older) with elevated blood pressure, type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk, defined by established cardiovascular disease, subclinical cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease or other cardiovascular risk factors. Patients were randomly assigned to intensive therapy targeting an SBP of less than 120 mm Hg or to standard therapy targeting an SBP of less than 140 mm Hg. The primary outcome was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure. Of 9,476 patients enrolled, 4,745 were assigned to intensive therapy and 4,731 to standard therapy. RESULTS: Mean SBP during follow-up was approximately 122 mm Hg in the intensive-therapy group and approximately 135 mm Hg in the standard-therapy group. Over a median follow-up of 4.0 years, the primary composite outcome occurred in 6.0% of patients in the intensive-therapy group and in 6.7% of patients in the standard-therapy group (hazard ratio, 0.90; P=0.20); the 95% confidence interval for this hazard ratio could not be confirmed by two independent sources and is therefore not reported here. The difference was not statistically significant. Rates of serious adverse events were similar in the two groups. Renal events were reported to be more frequent with intensive therapy, attributed mainly to a hemodynamic reduction in estimated glomerular filtration rate, although this was corroborated by only one source. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with type 2 diabetes, elevated blood pressure and high cardiovascular risk, targeting an SBP of less than 120 mm Hg did not reduce the incidence of major cardiovascular events as compared with a target of less than 140 mm Hg. The investigators explicitly caution that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that more intensive blood-pressure lowering is ineffective in people with type 2 diabetes: they suggest that any cardiovascular benefit may be smaller in diabetes than in people without diabetes, such that a trial of this size may not have been able to detect a modest yet clinically meaningful effect.

title: Implementation of Single-Pill Combination Therapy Through Team-Based Care for Hypertension Control in Resource-Constrained Settings: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract: IMPORTANCE: Single-pill combination therapy improves medication adherence and hypertension control. However, limited evidence is available on its implementation in routine clinical practice. OBJECTIVE: To assess the long-term effectiveness, implementation, and sustainability of single-pill combination therapy through team-based care for blood pressure reduction among patients with uncontrolled hypertension in primary care settings in Colombia and Jamaica. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Multicountry, unblinded, pragmatic, cluster randomized clinical trial. Twenty primary care clinics in Jamaica and 20 in Colombia were randomly assigned to either the single-pill combination therapy group or the standard care group. A total of 1706 adults with uncontrolled hypertension were enrolled between February 23, 2023, and September 12, 2024. The final follow-up visit occurred on September 9, 2026. INTERVENTIONS: In the intervention group (n = 869), a team-based care approach that included physician and nurse training, health coaching, home blood pressure monitoring, and blood pressure audit and feedback was used to implement single-pill combination therapy. Single-pill combinations were purchased locally and provided to patients. In the standard care group (n = 837), patients received monotherapy or polytherapy with guideline-recommended medications covered by health insurance or government programs. The intervention lasted 18 months, with additional follow-up at 24 months. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was the between-group difference in change in systolic blood pressure from baseline to 18 months. Three blood pressure measurements were obtained at each of 2 visits at each time point using a standard protocol. RESULTS: Among the 1706 enrolled participants, at baseline, the mean age was 61.4 years, 69.9% of participants were female, and 98.2% were taking antihypertensive medications. Among the 1574 participants included in the primary analysis, systolic blood pressure decreased by 19.1 mm Hg, from 145.9 mm Hg at baseline to 126.8 mm Hg at 18 months, in the intervention group and by 9.0 mm Hg, from 145.0 mm Hg to 136.1 mm Hg, in the standard care group, with a between-group difference of -10.1 mm Hg (95% CI, -13.3 to -6.9 mm Hg; P < .001). At 18 months, 69.5% of patients in the intervention group and 29.2% in the standard care group achieved systolic blood pressure less than 130 and diastolic blood pressure less than 80 mm Hg. Serious adverse events (death and hospitalization) occurred at similar frequencies in the intervention (7.9%) and standard care (9.9%) groups. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Implementing single-pill combination therapy through team-based care significantly reduced blood pressure over 18 months among adults with uncontrolled hypertension in Colombia and Jamaica. This comprehensive strategy integrating single-pill combination therapy with team-based care could be widely adopted and scaled up for hypertension control, particularly in resource-constrained settings. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05405920.

title: Effectiveness of Radiofrequency Renal Denervation in the United States: Six-Month Primary End Point Results From the SPYRAL AFFIRM Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Radiofrequency renal denervation (RDN) is a guideline-recommended therapy for uncontrolled hypertension. SPYRAL AFFIRM is a single-arm, postapproval study assessing the efficacy and safety of radiofrequency RDN using the Symplicity Spyral catheter. We report the 6-month primary end point results in the SPYRAL AFFIRM US population. METHODS: Enrolled patients had an office systolic/diastolic blood pressure (BP) ≥140/90 mm Hg and a home systolic BP ≥135 mm Hg. Patients with type 1 diabetes, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c >8.0%), or an estimated glomerular filtration rate <45 mL/min per 1.73 m2 were excluded. The primary end point was the 6-month change in office systolic BP from baseline compared with a prespecified performance goal (-6.0 mm Hg). RESULTS: Among 594 patients treated in the AFFIRM study from 73 US clinical sites, baseline clinical characteristics included: mean (±SD) age, 57±12 years; female, 45%; African American, 27%; Hispanic, 11%; type 2 diabetes, 19%; and mean estimated glomerular filtration rate, 79±20 mL/min per 1.73m2. Baseline systolic/diastolic office, home, and 24-hour ambulatory BP (mm Hg) were 169±21/106±13, 158±17/101±13, and 151±18/96±13, respectively. Patients were prescribed an average of 3.6±2.0 antihypertensive medications at baseline that remained unchanged through 6 months. Six months after RDN, the change in systolic BP (mm Hg) was -18.2±22.0, -9.4±13.8, and -9.7±16.8 for office, home, and 24-hour ambulatory measures, respectively (P<0.001 compared with baseline). Adverse clinical events through 6 months were uncommon. CONCLUSIONS: In this US postapproval study, the primary end point was met with significant BP reductions following radiofrequency RDN consistent across different measures. In a broader patient population with uncontrolled hypertension, these results reaffirm the safety and efficacy of radiofrequency RDN. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT05198674.

title: Impact of Statin and Aspirin Use on Dementia Diagnosis Stratified by Cardiovascular Risk
abstract: BACKGROUND: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) dementia share common risk factors. However, the role of ASCVD prevention therapies in AD dementia prevention is not fully understood. We examined the effect of LLT and antiplatelets with dementia and AD dementia diagnoses across ASCVD risk profiles. METHODS: We used data from primary prevention registry derived from a large healthcare network. Multivariable Cox proportional models were generated to study dementia and AD dementia diagnoses, stratified by ASCVD risk profiles. Impact of aspirin and LLT use on dementia and AD dementia diagnoses was assessed in adjusted models. RESULTS: Among n= 347,128, 2.4% developed dementia and 2.0% developed AD dementia over a median follow-up of 7.94 years. In adjusted models, dementia (HR, 2.59; 95% CI [2.29-2.92]) and AD dementia (HR, 2.85; 95% CI [2.49-3.25]) was higher in high risk patients. Low and high-dose aspirin among high ASCVD risk had lower dementia (HR, 0.88; 95% CI, [0.77-1.00] and HR, 0.83; 95% [CI 0.77-0.90]) and AD dementia (HR, 0.83; 95% CI [0.77-0.91] and HR, 0.85; 95% CI [0.73-0.97]). Similarly, moderate- to high-dose LLT use among high ASCVD risk groups was associated with lower dementia (HR, 0.85; 95% CI [0.79-0.93]) and AD dementia (HR, 0.85; 95% CI [0.78-0.93]). CONCLUSIONS: Higher baseline ASCVD risk was associated with increased risk of dementia and AD dementia diagnoses. Aspirin and moderate- to high-dose LLT use among patients with high ASCVD risk was associated with lower dementia and AD dementia risk.

title: Interleukin-6 Inhibition with Ziltivekimab for Atherosclerotic Disease
abstract: BACKGROUND: Residual inflammatory risk, marked by elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), persists in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) despite lipid-lowering therapy. Ziltivekimab is a fully human monoclonal antibody directed against the interleukin-6 (IL-6) ligand. The ZEUS trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05021835) tested whether IL-6 inhibition reduces cardiovascular events in patients with ASCVD, chronic kidney disease (CKD) and systemic inflammation. METHODS: ZEUS was a multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven trial. Eligible patients had established ASCVD together with CKD and an hs-CRP level of at least 2 mg/L. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to ziltivekimab 15 mg administered subcutaneously once monthly or to matching placebo. The primary endpoint was the time to first occurrence of 3-point MACE, a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction and nonfatal stroke. The full analysis population comprised 6,376 patients: 3,184 assigned to ziltivekimab and 3,192 assigned to placebo. Median baseline hs-CRP was 4.5 mg/L. RESULTS: Over a median follow-up of 33 months, the primary 3-point MACE endpoint occurred in 17.6% of patients assigned to ziltivekimab and in 17.7% of patients assigned to placebo (hazard ratio, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.88 to 1.11; P=0.84). All-cause mortality did not differ between groups. Ziltivekimab engaged its target as expected: at 24 months the between-group difference in median percent change in hs-CRP was approximately -64 percentage points, and IL-6 was likewise markedly reduced. Overall rates of adverse events and of serious adverse events were similar between the two groups (54.6% with ziltivekimab vs 54.8% with placebo). Serious infections were more frequent with ziltivekimab than with placebo (20.4% vs 17.9%), as were deaths attributed to infection (3.2% vs 2.5%) and serious venous thromboembolism (1.6% vs 0.6%). CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease and an hs-CRP level of at least 2 mg/L, once-monthly subcutaneous ziltivekimab 15 mg produced large reductions in IL-6 and hs-CRP but did not reduce the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events as compared with placebo, and was associated with an excess of serious infections. The investigators and commentators have emphasized that the neutral result does not in itself refute the inflammatory hypothesis of atherosclerosis.

title: Effects of semaglutide on cardiac structure and function in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity: a pre-specified cardiac magnetic resonance substudy of the CAMEO-SEMA trial
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists improve symptoms in patients with obesity and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). We recently demonstrated that semaglutide reduces exertional pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP) in obesity-related HFpEF, but potential effects of semaglutide on cardiac structure and function that may underlie these hemodynamic improvements remain unclear. In this prespecified cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) substudy of the randomized CAMEO-SEMA trial, 49 participants (33 semaglutide, 16 placebo, 28 female) underwent CMR at baseline and 52 weeks, within 1 day of invasive exercise hemodynamic assessment. The prespecified primary CMR endpoint was change in left atrial (LA) reservoir strain; other prespecified CMR endpoints included LV filling dynamics, which were assessed by early filling rate indexed to end-diastolic volume (eFR/EDV). Compared with placebo, semaglutide improved LA reservoir strain (+5.7% [95% CI, +0.3 to +9.7]; P=0.037) and eFR/EDV (+0.64 s-1 [95% CI, +0.42 to +1.00]; P<0.0001). Improvements in LA reservoir strain and LV filling dynamics were associated with reductions in exercise PAWP (r=-0.46, P<0.001 and r=-0.65, P<0.0001, respectively). With respect to other prespecified CMR endpoints, semaglutide reduced LV mass, restored more physiologic LV geometry, and improved right ventricular function and biventricular myocardial mechanics. The results of this CMR substudy indicate that in patients with obesity-related HFpEF, semaglutide improves LA function and LV diastolic filling dynamics, identifying improvements in myocardial function that may contribute to semaglutide's improvement of hemodynamics. ClinicalTrials.gov number: NCT05371496.

title: Implications of SGLT2 Inhibitors, GLP-1RAs, and Nonsteroidal MRAs on the Anticipated Burden of Heart Failure
abstract: BACKGROUND: Several treatments that reduce the risk of heart failure (HF) have been introduced recently. Their impact on the future burden of HF in the U.S. has not been well characterized. OBJECTIVES: This study aims to estimate the potential impact of recently approved cardiometabolic medications on the future burden of HF in the United States. METHODS: Using a nationally representative sample of persons in the United States 30-79 years of age without cardiovascular disease at baseline, we used the PREVENT (Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events) equation to estimate the 10- and 30-year burden of HF and the projected impact of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists on these estimates. The authors estimated the total number of HF cases that could be averted with risk-based treatment and calculated the number needed to treat to prevent HF. RESULTS: An estimated 5.5 million (95% CI: 5.1-5.8 million) U.S. adults 30-79 years of age without established cardiovascular disease will develop HF over 10 years. It is estimated to decrease to 5.1 million (95% CI: 4.7-5.4 million) with indicated treatment with a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor, 5.2 million (95% CI: 4.8-5.6 million) with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, 5.4 million (95% CI: 5.0-5.7 million) with nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and 4.8 million (95% CI: 4.4-5.2 million) with the use of combination therapy. The use of combination therapy in eligible persons with an estimated 10-year HF risk of ≥10% would result in 6.8 million (95% CI: 6.1-7.5 million) eligible participants, and 498,000 (95% CI: -663,000 to -319,000) fewer cases of HF, with a number needed to treat of 14 (95% CI: 10-22) to prevent 1 incident case. CONCLUSIONS: The projected burden of HF in the U.S. is substantial. A risk-based approach to preventive treatment may help reduce this considerably. The feasibility of such an approach deserves further investigation.

title: Obesity, frail obesity, and outcomes after durable left ventricular assist device implantation: a pooled analysis of the MOMENTUM 3 trials
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Obesity in patients supported by left ventricular assist devices (LVADs) is linked to excess mortality and haemocompatibility-related events. Whether this association persists with the fully magnetically levitated HeartMate 3 (HM3) pump is unknown. This analysis tested outcomes with obesity and the additive influence of co-existing frailty ('frail obesity') in the contemporary era. METHODS: The study pooled 2200 HM3 recipients from the MOMENTUM 3 pivotal randomized trial (n = 515) and Continued Access Protocol (n = 1685). Obesity was defined as body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m2 and frailty by a 40-item Rockwood cumulative-deficit frailty index (FI), with clinically relevant frailty defined as FI ≥0.325 (moderate-severe frailty); BMI was excluded from the FI to avoid mathematical coupling. The primary endpoint was survival to transplant, recovery, or 24 months of support free of disabling stroke (modified Rankin score >3) or pump replacement reoperation. RESULTS: Obese patients (n = 887, 40.3%) were younger, less often with ischaemic aetiology, and more frequently women, but more often had diabetes and hypertension, than non-obese patients. Unadjusted 2-year outcomes were similar between groups (freedom from the primary endpoint: 75.1% vs 77.1%, log-rank P = .34; survival: 79.9% vs 81.2%, P = .57). After covariate adjustment, obesity was independently associated with a higher risk of the primary endpoint (hazard ratio [HR] 1.30, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07-1.58) and all-cause mortality (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.10-1.67), as well as heart failure hospitalization, infection, and arrhythmia, but not stroke, bleeding, or early right heart failure. Frailty affected 67.3% of obese recipients (571/849) and was associated with a higher adjusted risk of the primary endpoint (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.09-2.10), overall mortality and non-haemocompatibilty-related morbidity endpoints. The obesity-by-frailty interaction was not significant for either the primary endpoint (P = .436) or mortality (P = .215), indicating additive rather than synergistic risk; frail-obese patients nonetheless carried the highest absolute risk of any subgroup. Frailty improved by at least one severity class by 6 months in 75.9% of frail-obese patients, and improvement was associated with better survival (adjusted HR 0.14, 95% CI 0.07-0.26). CONCLUSIONS: In the HM3 era, obese and non-obese recipients had similar unadjusted 2-year outcomes; however, after adjustment for baseline case-mix, obesity was independently associated with a higher risk of both the primary endpoint and all-cause mortality, together with heart failure hospitalization, infection, and arrhythmia. Frailty was independently associated with adverse outcomes across nearly all endpoints and was highly prevalent among obese recipients; the combination of obesity and frailty was additive but not synergistic, with frail-obese patients carrying the highest absolute risk. Frailty, however, proved substantially reversible after LVAD support, and its improvement was associated with markedly better survival. Obesity and frailty should therefore be assessed together, rather than through BMI thresholds alone, with recognition that frailty status is dynamic after implantation and that improvement in frailty is associated with markedly better survival.

title: Initial Diabetes Therapy After Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting and Long-Term Outcomes
abstract: BACKGROUND: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is common among patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), but optimal post-CABG glucose-lowering therapy remains uncertain. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the OptumLabs Data Warehouse of adults with T2D undergoing isolated CABG from 2012-2024. Follow-up began 30 days after discharge. Glucose-lowering therapy was modeled as a time-varying exposure with patients contributing no-observed-therapy person-time until the first qualifying post-discharge fill. Pairwise comparisons used stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality; secondary outcomes were heart failure hospitalization, stroke, and repeat coronary revascularization. RESULTS: Among 19,237 patients, 24.9% had no observed post-discharge therapy, 42.8% received metformin, 22.9% received insulin, and 9.4% received GLP-1RA/SGLT2i therapy. All active therapies were associated with lower mortality compared with no observed therapy, including GLP-1RA/SGLT2i (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.58-0.87), metformin (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.55-0.66), and insulin (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.67-0.84). Among active therapies, metformin was associated with lower mortality than insulin (HR, 0.61 [0.54-0.70]); GLP-1RA/SGLT2i comparisons with metformin and insulin were less precise. Metformin was also associated with lower cumulative incidence of heart failure hospitalization than no observed therapy and insulin, and lower stroke incidence than insulin. CONCLUSIONS: Observed glucose-lowering therapy initiation after CABG was associated with lower mortality compared with no observed therapy across all active treatment groups. These findings highlight a potential care gap and suggest that proper initiation of diabetes therapy after CABG represents an important opportunity to improve long-term outcomes following surgical revascularization.

title: Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a)
abstract: BACKGROUND: Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an independent, genetically determined risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, but it was unknown whether pharmacologic lowering of Lp(a) reduces cardiovascular events. Pelacarsen is an antisense oligonucleotide directed at hepatic apolipoprotein(a) synthesis. Lp(a)HORIZON (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04023552) was designed to test the Lp(a) hypothesis in secondary prevention. METHODS: Lp(a)HORIZON was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multinational trial conducted at 797 sites in 42 countries. Eligible patients had established cardiovascular disease, with a qualifying cardiovascular event between 3 months and 10 years before enrollment, and a baseline Lp(a) level of at least 70 mg/dL (approximately 148 nmol/L). Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to pelacarsen 80 mg administered subcutaneously once monthly or to matching placebo administered on the same schedule, on a background of guideline-directed therapy. Randomization was stratified by screening Lp(a) level so as to balance patients with Lp(a) of at least 90 mg/dL (approximately 192 nmol/L), who constituted a prespecified second primary analysis population. The primary endpoint was expanded major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE): a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, and urgent coronary revascularization. A total of 8,350 patients were randomly assigned and 8,322 were included in the efficacy analysis. RESULTS: Over a median follow-up of 4.7 years, the primary expanded-MACE endpoint occurred in 12.3% of patients assigned to pelacarsen and in 12.1% of patients assigned to placebo (hazard ratio, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.90 to 1.15). The exact P value for the primary comparison could not be verified in the available secondary sources and is therefore not reported here. The neutral result was consistent across the individual components of the composite. In the prespecified population with baseline Lp(a) of at least 90 mg/dL, the primary endpoint occurred in 12.3% of patients in each group (hazard ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.15). Pelacarsen had the expected biologic effect on its target: Lp(a) was reduced by 78.4% at 12 months, with a median Lp(a) at 12 months of 64.4 nmol/L with pelacarsen versus 233.4 nmol/L with placebo. Reported safety and tolerability details beyond the above (including rates of study-drug discontinuation, which were reported as higher with pelacarsen) could not be confirmed by two independent sources and are not reported here. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with established cardiovascular disease and an Lp(a) level of at least 70 mg/dL, pelacarsen 80 mg subcutaneously once monthly lowered Lp(a) by approximately 78% but did not reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events as compared with placebo over a median of 4.7 years. The investigators have stated that the findings were unexpected and disappointing and that they apply specifically to pelacarsen in a secondary-prevention setting, rather than invalidating Lp(a) as a causal risk factor.

title: Plozasiran for Severe Hypertriglyceridemia and Risk of Pancreatitis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Severe hypertriglyceridemia is associated with an increased risk of acute pancreatitis. Plozasiran, a small interfering RNA targeting APOC3 messenger RNA, lowers triglyceride levels and potentially mitigates the risk of acute pancreatitis. METHODS: In two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, 757 adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive plozasiran (25 mg) or placebo at baseline and at months 3, 6, and 9. These trials had identical designs, end points, and analytic plans. The primary end point was the percent change in the fasting plasma triglyceride level from baseline to month 12. Key secondary end points were the percent change in the fasting triglyceride level from baseline to month 10, a fasting triglyceride level of less than 500 mg per deciliter (5.6 mmol per liter) and less than 150 mg per deciliter (1.7 mmol per liter), the percent change in the fasting serum triglyceride level at month 12 for patients with a baseline triglyceride level of 880 mg per deciliter or greater, and changes in remnant cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol. A pooled analysis addressed adjudicated acute pancreatitis, incidence, and first-event timing. RESULTS: At month 12, patients in the plozasiran groups had a median triglyceride level that was lower than the baseline level by 79% and 81% in the two trials. These reductions corresponded to a median difference in the plozasiran groups as compared with the placebo groups (placebo-adjusted change) of -45 percentage points (95% confidence interval [CI], -51 to -38) and -47 percentage points (95% CI, -54 to -39). A triglyceride level of less than 500 mg per deciliter at 12 months was reported in 91% and 93% of the patients in the plozasiran groups and in 51% and 50% of those in the placebo groups (P<0.001). The rates of acute pancreatitis were 1 per 100 patient-years with plozasiran and 5 per 100 patient-years with placebo (rate ratio, 0.22; P = 0.008). Adverse events during treatment occurred in 73% of the patients in both the pooled plozasiran and placebo groups. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia, the use of plozasiran resulted in lower triglyceride levels and a lower risk of acute pancreatitis than placebo at 12 months. (Funded by Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals; SHASTA-3 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06347003; SHASTA-4, NCT06347016.).
